questions.problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+6xy+2$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x+6y & 2y+6x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2x+6y=0 \\ 2y+6x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+6(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2 \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2 \\  & =4+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (4+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{′} & =0 \\ 12\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{4},\,\frac{3\pi }{4},\,\frac{5\pi }{4},\,\frac{7\pi }{4}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain five candidate points:

$$
(\sqrt{2},0),\,(1,1),\,(-1,1),\,(-1,-1),\,(1,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(\sqrt{2},0)$ | $(1,1)$ | $(-1,1)$ | $(-1,-1)$ | $(1,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | $10$ | $-2$ | $10$ | $-2$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-2$ at the points $(-1,1)$ and $(1,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $10$ at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$

questions.problem: Find the global maximum of the function $f(x,y)=xy-x$ on the closed triangular region $D$ with vertices $(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}y-1 & x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}y-1=0 \\ x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,1).$ Since the point $(0,1)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,1).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =(t)(0)-(t) \\  & =-t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & =(0)(t)-(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,2).$

- The line connecting $(1,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0⟩+t(⟨0,2⟩-⟨1,0⟩) \\  & =⟨1,0⟩+t⟨-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨1-t,2t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(1-t,2t) \\  & =(1-t)(2t)-(1-t) \\  & =-2{t}^{2}+3t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,1),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (-2{t}^{2}+3t-1)^{′} & =0 \\ -4t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution. Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain one candidate point, $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2}).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain four candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(0,2),\,(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(1,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $\frac{1}{8}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2}).$

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=6x-2xy$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2-{x}^{2}/2},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}6-2y,\,-2x\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}6-2y=0 \\ -2x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,3).$ Since the point $(0,3)$ does not belong to the closed region of $D,$ we do not include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =6(t)-2(t)(0) \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the open interval $t\in (-2,2).$

- The parabola connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,2-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}⟩,\,t\in (-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,2-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =6(t)-2(t)(2-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}) \\  & ={t}^{3}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

 
To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-2,2),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{3}+2t)^{′} & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {t}^{2} & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation has no solution inside the interval $t\in (-2,2).$ So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points in the parabola connecting $(-2,0)$ and $(2,0).$

Finally, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain two candidates:

$$
(-2,0),\,(2,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(2,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-12$ | $12$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-12$ at the point $(-2,0)$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $12$ at the point $(2,0).$

questions.problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2y$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 3}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(0,-1)\in D.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(0,-1)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t+3{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (3+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives two solutions $t=\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain three candidate points:

$$
(\sqrt{3},0),\,(0,-\sqrt{3}),\,(0,\sqrt{3})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3},0) & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{0}^{2}+2(0) \\  & =3+0+0 \\  & =3 \\ f(0,-\sqrt{3}) & =(0)^{2}+(-\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3-2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3-2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,\sqrt{3}) & ={0}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =0+3+2\sqrt{3} \\  & =3+2\sqrt{3} \\ f(0,-1) & ={0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+2(-1) \\  & =0+1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-1$ at the point $(0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $3+2\sqrt{3}$ at the point $(0,\sqrt{3}).$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093615/assets/876ae377e99bbd69205e8118c881568859f5de8154d087f2fbfa1c4c06626249.png)

Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+{x}^{2}-2x+1$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,x\le 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve  ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x-2,\,2y\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(1,0).$ Since the point $(1,0)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(-3,0)$ and $(0,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (-3,0).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & ={0}^{2}+{t}^{2}-2t+1 \\  & ={t}^{2}-2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (-3,0),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}-2t+1)^{′} & =0 \\ 2t-2 & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution, $t=1$ is not inside the interval $t\in (-3,0).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,3)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,3).
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & ={t}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2(0)+1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,3),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({t}^{2}+1)^{′} & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution, $t=0$ is not inside the interval $t\in (0,3).$

- The quarter-circle connecting $(-3,0)$ and $(0,3)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨t,\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}}⟩,\,t\in (-3,0).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on this boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}}) \\  & ={(\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}})}^{2}+{t}^{2}-2t+1 \\  & =9-{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}-2t+1 \\  & =10-2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (-3,0).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, we obtain three candidates on the boundary:

$$
(-3,0),\,(0,0),\,(0,3)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(-3,0)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(0,3)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $16$ | $1$ | $10$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $1$ at the point $(0,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $16$ at the point $(-3,0).$
